repository.readme: Folio is an open-source Windows terminal. It typesets LaTeX where a command prints it, previews files beside the prompt, and marks the tab of an agent that is waiting for you. [中文说明](README.zh-CN.md) · [Shortcuts](docs/shortcuts.md) · [Security](SECURITY.md) · [Changes](CHANGELOG.md) > **Preview.** 0.3.0 is a preview build, signed by Weiyi Shi — see > [Download](#download) below. --- ## Download Take [`folio-0.3.0-windows-x64.zip`](https://github.com/lulu-loopp/folio-terminal/releases/download/v0.3.0-preview/folio-0.3.0-windows-x64.zip) from the [releases page](https://github.com/lulu-loopp/folio-terminal/releases), unpack it wherever you keep programs, and run `folio.exe`. There is no installer; keep the extracted files together in one folder. `SHA256SUMS.txt` is the hash of what you downloaded. Needs **Windows 10 1809 or newer, or Windows 11, 64-bit**. `folio.exe` and `folio.msix` are signed by **Weiyi Shi**, with a certificate from Microsoft's Artifact Signing service. On first run Windows may show **"Windows protected your PC"**. **"More info"** names the publisher: check that it reads **Weiyi Shi** before running it. The archive holds nine files that belong together: `folio.exe`, the two console libraries it needs to start a shell, `folio.msix` for the Explorer menu, `folio-here.cmd` for VS Code, and the licences and notices. The web preview needs the **WebView2 Runtime**. Windows 11 has it; Windows 10 usually does, and if it does not, the Evergreen Runtime is [here](https://developer.microsoft.com/microsoft-edge/webview2/). Without it everything except the web preview works, and the preview says what is missing. ## First run A machine that has never run Folio gets one card, once. It says **Welcome to Folio** and asks whether to check for updates, add Folio to the folder right-click menu, enable the PowerShell integration, and mark the tab for each of Claude Code, Codex and Copilot CLI this machine has. Update checks arrive on; the rest arrive off. Nothing about theme, font, size, language or layout — those are one click away and cost nothing while they are wrong. **Rest the pointer on a row and it says how** — including which of your own files the switch writes, and that the file is copied to a dated backup first. **Every row on the card is also a row in Settings**, so nothing on it is a last chance. **Done** applies the rows that are on. **Not now** and `Esc` keep the shipped values: the update check on, the rest off. Either way the card does not come back, and if you were already using Folio you never see it. The first tab opens the first shell your machine actually has. The five shipped profiles are looked for in order — PowerShell 7, Windows PowerShell, WSL, Git Bash, Command Prompt — and one whose program is not installed does not appear in the menus that start a shell; it stays on the Profiles page in Settings, greyed out and naming the program that was looked for. The seven agent profiles are found the same way, on the Windows path, and that is the same lookup the card's agent rows use. The PowerShell integration adds one line — `. "$env:APPDATA\Folio\shell-integration\folio.ps1"` — to the `$PROFILE` a PowerShell names for itself, after copying the file as it stood to a dated backup beside it; delete that line to undo it. Command marks and inline `$…$` formulas run on that integration. Git Bash and WSL need none of it. Where that file is comes from the shell, so a row left on when the card is answered takes effect in the next PowerShell session, and Settings > Terminal says so until it does. If you were not asked on the card, a strip offers the same thing the first time a PowerShell pane prints something: **Add to `$PROFILE`** does it, **Don't show again** ends the asking, and closing the strip decides nothing, so the next PowerShell asks once more. The three rows on the Agent page read the tool's own configuration file and report what is in it. On a new machine all three files are absent, so all three read Off. --- ## Features ### LaTeX rendering in the terminal The LaTeX a command prints is typeset where it was printed. - `$…$` and `$$…$$` in command output are set in the line the command printed them on. - The preview pane takes those, plus `\(…\)`, `\[…\]` and the bare `amsmath` environments. - Unsupported LaTeX remains visible as source text. - Inline `$…$` is told from a shell variable by the PowerShell integration below. Without it inline formulas stay as source, and `$$…$$` blocks still typeset. ### Made for agents The agent that is waiting for you is marked on its tab, so there is nothing to go and check. - A waiting agent lights a dot on its tab, flashes the taskbar if another program has the focus, and raises a Windows notification if the window is minimised or on another desktop. - One request interrupts at most once, and the dot clears when you answer in that pane or the program withdraws the request. `Ctrl+Shift+A` jumps to the longest wait. - Claude Code, Codex and GitHub Copilot CLI each have a switch on the Agent page in Settings that writes one notification hook into that tool's own configuration file and takes it back out again. Nothing is installed by default. - Seven profiles start an agent — Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Kimi Code, pi, Hermes, OpenCode — found on the Windows path; one installed inside WSL is run from the WSL profile. Any program that writes `OSC 1337;RequestAttention=yes` raises the mark, with nothing installed at all. ### Preview beside the prompt: files, PDF, video, web What is in a file is readable beside the prompt, without opening another application. - A card comes up under the pointer when it rests on a name in the files column: the PDF page by page, the video playing, the first lines of the text, the image itself. - The preview pane opens the file beside the prompt — markdown typeset, PDF page by page, video playing, a web page with an address field and Back. - A path the terminal printed opens in the preview pane on a click, and goes to the machine's own application on `Ctrl`+click. Paths nobody marked up are found too, once the file is confirmed to exist. - A web address follows the same rule: a click opens it in the preview pane, `Ctrl`+click hands it to the browser. - A window holds as many pages as it has preview panes. A second page opens on a pane of its own instead of navigating the first, so a page can be locked and another opened beside it, and a page dropped on a pane opens on the pane you dropped it on. ### Markdown you can edit where you read it A `.md` file is typed into on the page you were reading, in the typeface you were reading it in. - Click into a paragraph, heading, list or quote and it shows its own Markdown — the `#` of a heading, the `**` around a bold phrase, the `- ` in front of an item, the `> ` down the side of a quote — in the reading typeface and at the reading size, while every other block on the page stays as it reads. Leave the block and it is back to its rendered form. - A code block, a table or a formula turns to monospace source instead, because there the way the characters line up is part of what they say. - The caret moves between blocks the way it moves between lines, so there is nothing to enter and nothing to leave: arrows, `Home`, `End`, `Enter` and `Backspace` do what they do anywhere else. What you select is what you copy, and a copy out of a document you are editing brings the marks with it, so what you paste back is what was there. - `Ctrl+S` writes the file, `Ctrl+Z` takes back the last change and `Ctrl+Y` puts it again. A run of typing comes back in one press rather than a letter at a time, and the unsaved dot goes out when you undo back to your last save. - A save changes the part you edited and leaves the rest of the file identical, down to the byte. A file that names its own encoding in its first bytes — what Windows PowerShell writes is the common case — is written back in it. Line endings, trailing spaces and a missing last line break survive as they always did. - `Esc` leaves the page, and so does clicking the empty space beside the text or clicking away from the pane altogether. The page goes back to reading as a page, and the caret stays where you left it. - A file over 8 MB, and one Folio could not read as text all the way through, opens and reads and copies as before but is not edited; the foot of the pane says why. - The files column's right-click menu makes a file or a folder in place: `New file…` and `New folder…` put the name field in the tree where the new row will appear, `Enter` creates it and `Esc` cancels. A name the folder will not take turns red in the field rather than being explained somewhere else. `Delete` sends a file, or a whole folder, to the Recycle Bin and asks nothing first, because the Recycle Bin is where it goes. - Right-clicking the empty space in a files column opens the menu of the folder the column is standing in, so a folder with nothing in it can still be given its first file. - `Ctrl+Shift+P` finds a file under the folder the column is standing in, and `Enter` opens it in the preview pane, ready to be typed into. ### Panes, tabs and windows that move The layout changes while the sessions inside it keep running, and all of them can be seen at once. - `Alt+Shift+-` splits a pane across, `Alt+Shift+=` splits it down. A tab or a single pane can be dragged out into a window of its own, and the panes it did not touch keep their widths. - A pane dropped on the join between two tabs becomes a tab *between* them: a gap opens where it will land. Dropped on a tab itself it joins that tab's layout. The horizontal strip, the vertical rail and the card column all read the join the same way. - `Ctrl+Shift+Z` turns the tab strip into a column of cards, one per tab, each drawing that tab's own panes in the layout they have. - `Ctrl+Shift+G` turns the files column into a Git panel: branch, working tree, staged and unstaged files, the commit graph, and a selected file's diff in the preview. - `Ctrl+Shift+↑` and `Ctrl+Shift+↓` step between commands in the scrollback, and a command that failed is marked as having failed. - The folder button over the files column lists the folders your shells are standing in, then the last five folders you pointed a column at, each marked `recent`. ### A terminal on a hotkey One key brings a terminal down over whatever is on the screen, and the same key takes it away again. - ``Win+` `` drops a terminal across the top of whichever screen the pointer is on, over whatever was standing there. Pressing it again puts the window away and hands the keyboard back to the program it came down over. - It is the same Folio — tabs, panes, the files column, the preview, every shortcut — and it keeps its shells and its scrollback between summons. - A rectangle you move or resize by hand is remembered for the display it is on, so the summon comes down where you last put it on that screen. - It has no icon of its own, and closing the last window you can see ends the run. - **Settings > Summoned terminal** holds the key, which profile a new tab opens on, the height, width and the gap below the top of the screen, whether the window hides when the keyboard leaves it, and a command to run on the first summon of each run. - At the next launch a pinned tab's last command can come back typed at its prompt — typed, and not run. ### Search everything One box answers five questions at once, and `Enter` goes straight there. - `Ctrl+Shift+P` raises a box over the top of the window with five sections that never mix: what Folio can do, the panes and tabs this window has open, the commands it has run, the files under the folder its column is standing in, and the settings. - Typing narrows all five together and the arrow keys walk them. `Enter` on a pane raises it, on a file opens it in the preview pane, on a setting opens Settings at that row, and on an action does it. - A command still running is pointed at with a ring around the pane it is running in, rather than a scroll to a line that has gone past. - File search covers the folder the files column is showing. ### Windows integration - **Settings > General > Explorer context menu** puts Folio in the folder right-click menu, and On is everything your Windows can do. Windows 11 files "Open Folio here" under "Show more options"; on Windows 10 it stands in the only menu there is. On a Windows 11 with `folio.msix` beside `folio.exe`, On also puts "Open in Folio" on the page Windows 11 opens first. Off takes back whichever is registered, and the line under the row says which of them On reaches on your machine. A running File Explorer reads its list of first-page entries when it starts, so if "Open in Folio" is not there yet, sign out and back in. `docs/PRIVACY.md` lists what is written. If Folio is already running, the entry opens the folder as a new tab in the window you used last and brings that window forward — it asks for a terminal in a folder, not for another Folio, so it does that whatever **Settings > General > Opening Folio again** says. Starting Folio any other way opens a window, unless that row says otherwise. - Windows PowerShell 5.1 ships PSReadLine 2.0.0, which misplaces the input line after the window is resized. Folio carries a patched 2.4.6 and installs it into your module path on request. On a machine whose execution policy is still the stock `Restricted`, the switch says so and hands you the `Set-ExecutionPolicy` command that lets the module load. ### Visual Studio Code `folio-here.cmd` ships in the archive, beside `folio.exe`, and is one line: ```bat @"%~dp0folio.exe" --from-here --cwd "%CD%" ``` Point VS Code's external terminal at it — Settings, or `settings.json`: ```json "terminal.external.windowsExec": "C:\\Tools\\folio\\folio-here.cmd" ``` **Terminal > Open in External Terminal** (`Ctrl+Shift+C`) then opens Folio on the folder the editor is standing in. The `.cmd` exists because that setting runs a command with no arguments, and `--cwd` is how Folio is told where to start; `--from-here` says that this is a terminal in a folder rather than another Folio, so it arrives as a tab in the window you used last whatever **Settings > General > Opening Folio again** says. --- ## Privacy Folio has no telemetry, no analytics and no crash reporting. There is no model and no API key in it; it serves the agents you already run. Two things reach the network: a page you open in the web preview, and the update check. The update check is one `GET` of `https://api.github.com/repos/lulu-loopp/folio-terminal/releases`, at most once a day across every window, carrying a `User-Agent` of `Folio` and nothing else: no version, no identifier, no query string. What it can do with the answer is draw a mark on the settings gear and a line in Settings; it downloads nothing and replaces nothing. Switch it off at Settings > General > **Update check**, or with `"update_check": false` in `settings.json`. What it remembers lives in two directories: `%APPDATA%\Folio` for settings, profiles, schemes and the session, and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Folio\WebView2` for the web preview's cookies and cache. Delete the first and Folio starts as it did new. ```powershell Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:APPDATA\Folio" Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Folio\WebView2" ``` What is in each file, and why a full address ends up in `session.json`, is in [`docs/PRIVACY.md`](docs/PRIVACY.md). ## Known issues - **A window was once reported drawing its top half black** after a move to a second monitor, unreproduced. Attach `%APPDATA%\Folio\diagnostics.log` if you hit it. - **`.webm` needs the VP9 or AV1 Video Extension** from the Microsoft Store. A stock Windows has neither, and without one there is no still and no playback. - The rest are in [`CHANGELOG.md`](CHANGELOG.md). ## Licence MIT or Apache-2.0, at your option. Every dependency's licence and the notices they require are in [`THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md`](THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md). The two licences grant copyright and patent permissions and nothing else. The Folio name and the marks are not covered — [`TRADEMARK.md`](TRADEMARK.md) says what that means for a modified distribution. ## Building and contributing Building from source is in [`docs/BUILDING.md`](docs/BUILDING.md); [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md) is how a change gets made; security reports go through the private channel in [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md), not an issue. ## What's next - macOS, then Linux. - The terminal from a phone. These are directions, not dates.

sampled_files..github/workflows/ci.yml:
name: CI

on:
  push:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always
  # A build here is a fresh one every time; incremental artefacts are pure cost
  # in a job whose target directory arrives from a cache and leaves with it.
  CARGO_INCREMENTAL: 0

# `windows-2025` and not `windows-latest`. The floating label moved from Server
# 2022 to Server 2025 during this project's life and will move again; a terminal
# emulator's CI is a statement about a Windows version, and a statement that
# silently changes what it is about is not one.
#
# Third-party actions are pinned to a commit, not a tag: a tag is a name its
# owner can repoint, and these actions run with the checkout of this repository
# in front of them.

jobs:
  # ── the three gates that prove themselves ──────────────────────────────────
  #
  # Each of these plants a violation, demands red, and puts the file back. This
  # repository has shipped a gate that could not fail, plus a comment that lied
  # about it, plus a lint table that inherited into nothing; a green run means
  # nothing until the red one has been seen.
  #
  # **Every step here ends with an explicit `exit 0`, and that is load-bearing.**
  # A canary runs a command whose *failure is the thing it is checking for*, and
  # GitHub's `pwsh` shell appends `if (Test-Path variable:\LASTEXITCODE) { exit
  # $LASTEXITCODE }` to the script it runs. Without the explicit exit, the probe's
  # refusal becomes the step's own — the lint canary proved on the first CI run
  # that clippy does reject a planted `todo!()`, and then reported that proof as
  # a red step with nothing in its log, because clippy's 101 was still sitting in
  # `$LASTEXITCODE` when the script ran out. The probe's exit code is read into a
  # variable of its own and never left where the shell will find it.
  gates-can-fail:
    runs-on: windows-2025
    # The ignored-test probe has to build the whole workspace before it can ask
    # the harness anything, which is why this is not the five minutes the
    # adapter-boundary check alone would need.
    timeout-minutes: 60
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4
      # The compiler and the shared cache both come from
      # `.github/actions/toolchain`, which is the one place in this repository
      # that decides what Rust a job is built with. `release.yml` calls the same
      # action, so the two files cannot drift apart again.
      - uses: ./.github/actions/toolchain

      # adapter.rs/cell_capture.rs are the vendor compatibility seam. Their job is to report
      # terminal facts; importing document, detection, or viewport policy here recreates the
      # layering bug Task 00b removed.
      - name: the adapter boundary gate can actually fail
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $file = "crates/bt-term/src/adapter.rs"
          $original = [IO.File]::ReadAllText($file)
          try {
            [IO.File]::AppendAllText($file, "`nuse bt_doc::HistoryDocument as _AdapterBoundaryProbe;`n")
            $failed = $false
            try {
              & ./scripts/check-adapter-boundary.ps1 *> $null
            } catch {
              $failed = $true
            }
            if (-not $failed) {
              throw "adapter boundary check accepted a planted bt_doc import"
            }
          } finally {
            [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $original)
          }
          exit 0

      # The portable core is thirteen crates that must go on compiling on the two
      # platforms this workflow has one job each on.
      # `scripts/check-portable-core.ps1` is the cheap half of that guard and
      # `core-macos` and `core-linux` are the compiling half; this proves the
      # cheap half is not decoration.
      - name: the portable-core gate can actually fail
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $file = "crates/bt-doc/src/lib.rs"
          $original = [IO.File]::ReadAllText($file)
          try {
            [IO.File]::AppendAllText($file, "`nuse windows::Win32::Foundation::HANDLE as _PortableCoreProbe;`n")
            $failed = $false
            try {
              & ./scripts/check-portable-core.ps1 *> $null
            } catch {
              $failed = $true
            }
            if (-not $failed) {
              throw "the portable-core check accepted a planted windows:: import"
            }
          } finally {
            [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $original)
          }
          exit 0

      # The same script's *second* check, and a separate canary because it is a
      # separate rule with a separate list: `bt-app` may know what platform it
      # is on, and `main.rs`'s own `FILES_THAT_MAY_NAME_A_PLATFORM` says in which
      # files. The violation is planted in a file that is not on that list, which
      # is the only shape this check refuses. Note that the *first* check runs
      # first and passes — `bt-app` is not one of the thirteen portable crates —
      # so a red here is this rule's red and nobody else's.
      - name: the bt-app platform-gate check can actually fail
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $file = "crates/bt-app/src/notice.rs"
          $original = [IO.File]::ReadAllText($file)
          try {
            [IO.File]::AppendAllText($file, "`n#[cfg(windows)]`nfn _platform_gate_probe() {}`n")
            $failed = $false
            try {
              & ./scripts/check-portable-core.ps1 *> $null
            } catch {
              $failed = $true
            }
            if (-not $failed) {
              throw "the gate accepted a platform cfg in a bt-app file that is not on the list"
            }
          } finally {
            [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $original)
          }
          exit 0

      - name: the lint gate can actually fail
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $file = "crates/bt-doc/src/lib.rs"
          $original = [IO.File]::ReadAllText($file)
          $clippy = $null
          try {
            [IO.File]::AppendAllText($file, "`nfn _lint_gate_probe() { todo!() }`n")
            cargo clippy -p bt-doc --locked -- -D warnings 2>&1 | Out-Null
            $clippy = $LASTEXITCODE
          } finally {
            [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $original)
          }
          if ($clippy -eq 0) {
            throw "clippy passed a planted todo!() - workspace lints are not reaching this crate ([lints] workspace = true missing?)"
          }
          Write-Host "clippy refused the planted todo!() with exit $clippy, which is this gate passing."
          exit 0

      # A newly ignored test has to be a newly listed test. Planting one proves
      # the comparison is two-way and that the exit code is read before the
      # output — the two things the phrase-matching gate this replaced got
      # wrong. See `scripts/ci/check-ignored-tests.ps1`.
      - name: the ignored-test gate can actually fail
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $file = "crates/bt-doc/src/lib.rs"
          $original = [IO.File]::ReadAllText($file)
          try {
            [IO.File]::AppendAllText($file, "`n#[test]`n#[ignore = `"planted`"]`nfn _ignored_gate_probe() {}`n")
            $failed = $false
            try {
              & ./scripts/ci/check-ignored-tests.ps1
            } catch {
              $failed = $true
            }
            if (-not $failed) {
              throw "the allowlist accepted a test that is not on it"
            }
          } finally {
            [IO.File]::WriteAllText($file, $original)
          }
          exit 0

  # ── everything that is decided by reading, not by hardware ────────────────
  logic:
    runs-on: windows-2025
    timeout-minutes: 45
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4
      # The compiler and the shared cache both come from
      # `.github/actions/toolchain`, which is the one place in this repository
      # that decides what Rust a job is built with. `release.yml` calls the same
      # action, so the two files cannot drift apart again.
      - uses: ./.github/actions/toolchain

      - name: adapter modules do not import policy crates
        shell: pwsh
        run: ./scripts/check-adapter-boundary.ps1

      # The other boundary, and the other platform. See the script's own header
      # and `docs/DESIGN.md` §Portability.
      - name: the portable core calls no Win32 outside a cfg(windows) gate
        shell: pwsh
        run: ./scripts/check-portable-core.ps1

      # vendor/alacritty_terminal must stay a workspace member: its own upstream
      # suite is our regression line against our patches breaking VT semantics,
      # and it only runs while it is a member. A real regression hid behind
      # exactly this gap — see docs/reviews/claude-review-M-1-part1-rework.md.
      #
      # Asked of cargo, not of a grep: the manifest mentions this path twice
      # (members and [patch.crates-io]), so grepping it passes even with the
      # member deleted.
      - name: vendored alacritty is a workspace member at the pinned version
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $meta = cargo metadata --format-version 1 --no-deps --locked | ConvertFrom-Json
          $want = [IO.Path]::GetFullPath("vendor/alacritty_terminal/Cargo.toml", $PWD.Path)
          $pkg = $meta.packages | Where-Object {
            $_.name -eq "alacritty_terminal" -and
            [IO.Path]::GetFullPath($_.manifest_path) -eq $want
          }
          if (-not $pkg) { throw "vendored alacritty_terminal is not in the workspace" }
          if ($pkg.id -notin $meta.workspace_members) {
            throw "vendored alacritty_terminal left workspace.members - its upstream tests would stop running"
          }
          if ($pkg.version -ne "0.26.0") { throw "vendored alacritty is $($pkg.version), expected 0.26.0" }

      # First-party only: vendor is upstream's code in upstream's format, and
      # reformatting it would bury our patches in 300 lines of whitespace diff.
      # Every first-party package, because a crate left off this list is a crate
      # whose formatting nothing checks.
      - name: fmt
        run: >
          cargo fmt
          --package bt-term --package bt-transcript --package bt-doc
          --package bt-viewport --package bt-detect --package bt-corpus
          --package bt-layout --package bt-math --package bt-pty
          --package bt-platform --package bt-persist --package bt-unicode
          --package bt-render --package bt-winres --package bt-app
          -- --check

      - name: clippy
        run: cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings

      # Ours and alacritty's upstream suite in one go, because vendor is a
      # member — minus the two crates whose tests are about hardware. `bt-pty`
      # starts real ConPTY sessions and `bt-render` asks for a real adapter;
      # each has a job of its own below, where the machine it needs is set up
      # and where a failure means something specific.
      - name: test
        run: cargo test --workspace --locked --exclude bt-pty --exclude bt-render

      - name: the ignored tests are exactly the ones on the list
        shell: pwsh
        run: ./scripts/ci/check-ignored-tests.ps1

      # `check-vendor-notices.ps1` reads upstream alacritty 0.26.0 out of the
      # registry to diff it against `vendor/`, so the sources have to be there.
      # A no-op after the build above; named anyway, because a job that only
      # works because of what a previous step happened to leave behind is a job
      # that breaks when the steps are reordered.
      - name: fetch the sources the notices gates read
        run: cargo fetch --locked

      # `check-notices.ps1` regenerates `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md` and compares
      # bytes, and the generator is `cargo about`. Without this the gate below
      # does not report drift — it reports a missing tool, which is a different
      # failure wearing the same red. Pinned to the version the checked-in file
      # was generated with: a newer one that renders a heading differently would
      # read as drift in the licences rather than a change in the renderer.
      - name: cargo-about
        run: cargo install cargo-about --locked --version 0.9.2 --features cli

      # The three gates the licensing line owns: the generated third-party
      # notices still match the lock file, no machine path or personal name is
      # tracked, and every modified vendored file carries its Apache-2.0 §4(b)
      # notice. Each says so and is skipped when it is not in the tree — this
      # branch and that one land separately, and a missing file is not a
      # violation.
      - name: the licensing line's gates
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          $gates = @(
            "scripts/check-notices.ps1",
            "scripts/check-machine-paths.ps1",
            "scripts/check-doc-words.ps1",
            "scripts/check-vendor-notices.ps1"
          )
          $ran = 0
          foreach ($gate in $gates) {
            if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $gate)) {
              Write-Warning "$gate is not in the tree yet - it did not run"
              continue
            }
            Write-Host "== $gate"
            pwsh -NoLogo -NoProfile -File $gate
            if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "$gate failed with exit $LASTEXITCODE" }
            $ran++
          }
          Write-Host "$ran of $($gates.Count) licensing gates ran."

  # ── real ConPTY, real child processes ─────────────────────────────────────
  conpty:
    runs-on: windows-2025
    timeout-minutes: 30
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4
      # The compiler and the shared cache both come from
      # `.github/actions/toolchain`, which is the one place in this repository
      # that decides what Rust a job is built with. `release.yml` calls the same
      # action, so the two files cannot drift apart again.
      - uses: ./.github/actions/toolchain

      # These spawn cmd.exe and powershell.exe through the sidecar ConPTY that
      # `crates/bt-pty/build.rs` extracts, and read what comes back. They are
      # the only tests in this workspace that can fail because of what the
      # operating system did.
      - name: test bt-pty against real child processes
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          cargo test -p bt-pty --locked 2>&1 | Tee-Object -FilePath conpty-tests.log
          if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "bt-pty tests failed" }

      - name: the sidecar is the one that was extracted
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          foreach ($name in @("conpty.dll", "OpenConsole.exe")) {
            $path = "target/debug/$name"
            if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $path)) { throw "$path was not extracted" }
            "{0,12:N0}  {1}" -f (Get-Item $path).Length, $path | Write-Host
          }

      - if: failure()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@ea165f8d65b6e75b540449e92b4886f43607fa02 # v4
        with:
          name: conpty-failure
          path: conpty-tests.log
          if-no-files-found: ignore

  # ── a real adapter, which a runner does not have until one is installed ────
  gpu:
    runs-on: windows-2025
    timeout-minutes: 40
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4
      # The compiler and the shared cache both come from
      # `.github/actions/toolchain`, which is the one place in this repository
      # that decides what Rust a job is built with. `release.yml` calls the same
      # action, so the two files cannot drift apart again.
      - uses: ./.github/actions/toolchain

      # The test binaries have to exist before WARP can be put beside them:
      # DXGI prefers a `d3d10warp.dll` in the loading binary's own directory,
      # which is `target/debug/deps`.
      - name: build the render tests
        run: cargo test -p bt-render --locked --no-run

      - name: install WARP
        shell: pwsh
        run: ./scripts/ci/install-warp.ps1 -TargetDir target/debug

      - name: test bt-render on a real device
        run: cargo test -p bt-render --locked

  # ── the executable, started ───────────────────────────────────────────────
  #
  # Every gate above runs against a library. This one runs `folio.exe`: the
  # front door's exit codes, a cold launch that opens a window and gets text
  # onto it, the ConPTY it actually loaded, and whether it agrees with Windows
  # about its own DPI. A runner has no WebView2 Runtime, which makes it exactly
  # the machine the preview's degrade path has to be right on.
  smoke:
    runs-on: windows-2025
    timeout-minutes: 60
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4
      # The compiler and the shared cache both come from
      # `.github/actions/toolchain`, which is the one place in this repository
      # that decides what Rust a job is built with. `release.yml` calls the same
      # action, so the two files cannot drift apart again.
      - uses: ./.github/actions/toolchain

      - name: build folio.exe
        run: cargo build -p bt-app --locked

      - name: install WARP
        shell: pwsh
        run: ./scripts/ci/install-warp.ps1 -TargetDir target/debug

      - name: start it
        shell: pwsh
        run: ./scripts/release/smoke.ps1 -Exe target/debug/folio.exe -Artifacts target/smoke -TimeoutSeconds 300

      - if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@ea165f8d65b6e75b540449e92b4886f43607fa02 # v4
        with:
          name: smoke
          path: target/smoke
          if-no-files-found: warn

  # ── the second platform, kept from drifting away by compiling it ──────────
  #
  # `docs/plans/port/macos-spike-2026-09-07.md` measured that about 90 % of this
  # workspace already builds on macOS, and that what stands between it and the
  # rest is one crate — `bt-platform` — plus the modules of `bt-app` that consume
  # it. A macOS port is its own milestone and it is not scheduled. **This job is
  # not that port.** It exists because the measurement has a half-life: every
  # feature landed on a Windows-only CI can add a Win32 call to a portable crate
  # and nothing will say so, and the 90 % is then a number about a day in
  # September rather than about this repository.
  #
  # So the crates are named one at a time — the thirteen
  # `scripts/check-portable-core.ps1` names, plus the vendored terminal they are
  # all downstream of, plus `bt-platform` and `bt-app`, which that script does
  # not name because they are the two crates that *may* know what platform they
  # are on. The reason is the same for all of them: "everything" is a shape a
  # script can infer, while "these are the crates we promise compile on a second
  # platform" is a decision. A crate that joins the workspace joins this list on
  # purpose, or the promise does not cover it.
  #
  # It is required in the same sense every other job here is: nothing in this
  # file is `continue-on-error`, and `gates-can-fail` differs from its neighbours
  # by *proving itself* rather than by being optional. A red here is a red run.
  #
  # **M1-10 grew this job from thirteen crates to the whole of what compiles.**
  # The two sentences that used to stand here — "`bt-app` is deliberately absent
  # and is expected to fail: 321 errors naming 79 items missing from
  # `bt_platform`" and "moving `bt-pty` onto the test line is M1-10's job,
  # together with the `-D warnings` line" — were both true when they were
  # written and are both retired. M1-1 gave `bt_platform` the missing items and
  # `bt-app` links here; M1-6 ran `bt-pty`'s suite against real Unix children on
  # the owner's Mac mini; M1-10 fixed the last three `bt-app` targets that only
  # `--all-targets` ever compiles, and cleared the warnings the `-D warnings`
  # line tripped over.
  #
  # So what this job now proves, in the order the steps make the claims:
  #
  # ① the fifteen crates below compile on macOS with their test code, which is
  #    the promise `core-linux` makes in the same words;
  # ② **`bt-app` compiles here, every target of it** — the binary, its test
  #    target and both video probes in `examples/`. `--all-targets` is the whole
  #    point: a `#[cfg(test)]` module and an example are where a platform
  #    assumption hides most cheaply, and the three targets M1-10 fixed were
  #    exactly those;
  # ③ twelve suites run, `bt-platform`'s and `bt-pty`'s among them — the second
  #    starts real Unix children over a real pty, which is a thing no Windows job
  #    in this file can do;
  # ④ `bt-platform` passes clippy with `-D warnings`, which is the lint line
  #    `logic` holds on Windows, held on the platform where half that crate is a
  #    refusal.
  #
  # What is still checked and not tested, and why: `bt-render` asks for a real
  # adapter and a runner has none (the `gpu` job above is where that question is
  # asked); `bt-term` and `bt-corpus` because nobody has measured their suites on
  # a second platform, and a list of what we have measured is worth more than a
  # list of what we hope. **`bt-app` is checked and not tested on purpose**: its
  # suite is 3,498 tests and most of them want a window, a renderer or a ConPTY,
  # and turning that on here would be a different ticket with a different
  # acceptance line rather than a longer command.
  core-macos:
    runs-on: macos-latest
    timeout-minutes: 45
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4
      # The same composite action every other job comes through. It reads the
      # channel out of rust-toolchain.toml and, off Windows, installs that
      # version against this runner's own host triple — the pin is the version,
      # and the triple in that file settles which of the two Windows hosts a
      # Windows machine picks.
      - uses: ./.github/actions/toolchain

      # `--all-targets`, because the test code is where a platform assumption
      # hides most cheaply: five of the seven errors this branch fixed were in
      # `#[cfg(test)]` modules that had never been compiled anywhere else.
      #
      # The same fifteen `core-linux` checks and in the same order, for the
      # reason that job's own comment gives: two lists that mean one thing
      # drift, and a diff that changes one and not the other is meant to be read
      # as the mistake it is.
      - name: check the portable crates
        run: >
          cargo check --locked --all-targets
          -p bt-unicode -p bt-doc -p bt-detect -p bt-layout -p bt-persist
          -p bt-winres -p bt-math -p bt-transcript -p bt-viewport
          -p bt-render -p bt-term -p bt-pty -p bt-corpus -p bt-platform
          -p alacritty_terminal

      # **The application, every target of it** (M1-10). A step of its own and
      # not a name on the line above, because the claim is a different one: the
      # list above is "the core still compiles somewhere that is not Windows"
      # and this is "the product does". It is also the step whose red is worth
      # reading on its own — `bt-app` is where the port actually happens, and a
      # failure buried in a fifteen-crate command names a crate rather than a
      # milestone.
      #
      # `--all-targets` reaches three targets nothing else compiles: the bin's
      # own `#[cfg(test)]` modules and the two probes in `examples/`, which name
      # DirectComposition and Media Foundation and are `#[cfg(windows)]` per item
      # with a portable `main` beside them. Those three were the whole of what
      # M1-1 left failing here.
      - name: check the application, every target of it
        run: cargo check --locked --all-targets -p bt-app

      # The eight suites the spike's own table records as green here, plus the
      # two M1-1's branch made green — `bt-transcript` and `bt-viewport`, whose
      # seven failures were all one cause: a path grammar that only knew Windows
      # — plus the two M1-10 added.
      #
      # **`bt-platform` and `bt-pty` are the two this ticket moved from `check`
      # to `test`, and they are the two that matter most here.** `bt-platform`
      # off Windows is mostly refusals, and a refusal that is never called is a
      # claim nobody has read back: `portable_impl::refusal_tests` calls every
      # door, and the four fixture-gated rules M1-10 mirrored (the trailing-dot
      # trim, the reveal argument, where a program is looked for, the Explorer
      # registration) each have a POSIX twin that only runs here and on Linux.
      # `bt-pty` starts real Unix children over a real pty — spawn, resize, exit
      # and reap — which M1-6 measured on the owner's Mac mini and which no
      # Windows job in this file can do.
      - name: test the portable crates
        run: >
          cargo test --locked
          -p bt-unicode -p bt-doc -p bt-detect -p bt-layout -p bt-persist
          -p bt-winres -p bt-math -p bt-transcript -p bt-viewport
          -p bt-platform -p bt-pty -p alacritty_terminal

      # **The lint line, held on the second platform** (M1-10). `logic` runs
      # `clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` on Windows, and until
      # this ticket nothing held that bar anywhere else: M1-6 reported
      # `bt-platform` and `bt-transcript` red here on Windows-only dead code,
      # which is how a `#[cfg(windows)]` that should have been written gets
      # noticed at all.
      #
      # `bt-platform` and not the workspace, for now. It is the crate the port
      # is about and the one whose non-Windows half is written rather than
      # inherited; widening this to the crates above is cheap and is a decision
      # somebody should take on purpose rather than a flag that grew.
      - name: the lint line on bt-platform
        run: cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -p bt-platform -- -D warnings

  # ── the platform the remote work runs on ──────────────────────────────────
  #
  # `docs/plans/remote/research-2026-09-10.md` §1 puts 0.4 on a Unix box: the
  # Folio that owns the shells lives there and the local one drives it, and what
  # that server takes from this workspace is the portable core plus `bt-pty` —
  # "everything — spawn, write, resize, read, wait, the output ring" (§1's
  # table). `core-macos` above proves the core still compiles somewhere that is
  # not Windows; this proves it where the next milestone's code will actually
  # run, and it does so before that code exists rather than after.
  #
  # The label floats, as it does on the mac job and unlike `windows-2025`. The
  # rule at the top of this file is about a *Windows version*, because that is
  # what a terminal emulator's behaviour is a statement about; this job's claim
  # is "a Linux userland compiles and runs this", which no Ubuntu release number
  # narrows usefully.
  #
  # **The one thing this job does that `core-macos` does not is test `bt-pty`,
  # and Linux is why it can.** The reason that crate is off the mac test line —
  # and off the `logic` job's — is that its suite "starts real child processes
  # through a ConPTY that does not exist off Windows". That is two claims wearing
  # one coat, and Linux takes them apart: it has no ConPTY either, but it has a
  # *real pty*, and `vendor/conpty/portable-pty` still carries the `#[cfg(unix)]`
  # `UnixPtySystem` over `libc::openpty` that `bt-pty` reaches through
  # `native_pty_system()` (research §2). So the crate's portable half runs here
  # for the first time: the output ring and its backpressure, the input ring and
  # the writer thread that is the only thing allowed to meet the pipe, the reader
  # that drains a closed ring so a shutdown cannot deadlock, the bounded reap,
  # the recorder and its chunk sidecar, and the interpreter grammar.
  #
  # What does **not** run here is the half that needs a Windows child —
  # `cmd.exe`, `powershell.exe`, and the shell resolution whose whole answer is
  # `pwsh.exe` or `powershell.exe`. Those tests carry `#[cfg(windows)]` and the
  # `conpty` job above is where they run; a fixture in them is a Windows path and
  # a `PATH` a Unix `join_paths` refuses, so they were never platform-neutral
  # tests that happened to be run in one place.
  #
  # **This job starts processes now** (M1-6, which is also remote T2).
  # `resolve_default_shell` has the Unix rule the remote server needs — `$SHELL`
  # when it names a program this machine can start, then the system shells this
  # platform is probed for, then `/bin/sh`, interactive and non-login — and the
  # PowerShell arguments and the PowerShell retry are `#[cfg(windows)]` and
  # unreachable from here. So the `#[cfg(unix)]` half of `bt-pty`'s suite spawns
  # `/bin/sh` over a real pty and asks this runner's own kernel the five
  # questions nobody had asked it: that a child's output reaches the output ring,
  # that its chosen exit code survives the trip and the process is reaped rather
  # than left a zombie (read back out of `ps`, not out of our own bookkeeping),
  # that a resize is a real `TIOCSWINSZ` the child sees in its own `stty size`,
  # that a child which has trapped `SIGHUP` away and carried that disposition
  # through an `exec` is ended anyway when its session goes, and that shutting a
  # session down hands the child a newline before any of that — which is the
  # vendored backend's `UnixMasterWriter::drop`, has no Windows counterpart, and
  # was found by this ticket rather than known. Ubuntu has `/bin/sh`,
  # `/bin/bash`, `sleep`, `stty` and `ps`, which is the whole of what they need.
  core-linux:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 45
    # **The static C runtime is a Windows shipping rule and this job ships
    # nothing.** `.cargo/config.toml` puts `-C target-feature=+crt-static` on
    # every build so that `folio.exe` carries its own CRT rather than asking a
    # clean machine for the Visual C++ redistributable, and it says `[build]`
    # rather than a target table on purpose — the flag has to reach build
    # scripts and proc macros there too. macOS ignores the feature. Linux does
    # not: glibc honours it, and a statically linked host cannot load a dynamic
    # library, so the first proc macro in the graph stops the compile with
    # "cannot produce proc-macro for `bytecheck_derive` as the target
    # x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu does not support these crate types". `RUSTFLAGS`
    # outranks the config file, and it says the opposite here rather than
    # nothing, so that a reader sees a decision instead of an omission.
    env:
      RUSTFLAGS: -C target-feature=-crt-static
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11d5960a326750d5838078e36cf38b85af677262 # v4
      # The same composite action every other job comes through, and off Windows
      # it installs the pinned *version* against this runner's own host triple.
      - uses: ./.github/actions/toolchain

      # The same fifteen crates `core-macos` checks and in the same order,
      # because they are the same promise: `scripts/check-portable-core.ps1`'s
      # thirteen, plus the vendored terminal they are all downstream of, plus
      # `bt-platform` (M1-10). Two lists that mean one thing drift; a diff that
      # changes one and not the other is meant to be read as the mistake it is.
      #
      # **`bt-platform` is here and `bt-app` is not, and the asymmetry is the
      # point.** §4.6 of `docs/plans/port/macos-plan-2026-09-12.md` states the
      # rule the remote server inherits: the macOS GUI dependencies are declared
      # only for macOS targets, so a Linux build of this crate links *nothing* —
      # `Cargo.toml`'s dependency table is empty outside the two platform
      # sections. Checking it here is what turns that from a manifest one can
      # read into a claim a machine has answered, and it is the only place in
      # this file where it is answered at all. `bt-app` stays off: the server
      # never depends on it (§4.6, unconditional), and a Linux build of the
      # application is a milestone nobody has scheduled.
      - name: check the portable crates
        run: >
          cargo check --locked --all-targets
          -p bt-unicode -p bt-doc -p bt-detect -p bt-layout -p bt-persist
          -p bt-winres -p bt-math -p bt-transcript -p bt-viewport
          -p bt-render -p bt-term -p bt-pty -p bt-corpus -p bt-platform
          -p alacritty_terminal

      # `core-macos`'s ten, plus `bt-pty` for the reason above and minus
      # `bt-math` for one of the same shape. `bt-render` is still checked and not
      # tested: it asks for a real adapter, and a runner without one is a
      # different failure wearing the same red. `bt-term` and `bt-corpus` stay
      # off for the reason the mac job gives — nobody has measured their suites
      # on a second platform, and a list of what we have measured is worth more
      # than a list of what we hope.
      #
      # **`bt-math` asks the machine for fonts, and this one has none worth the
      # name.** Three of its tests are deliberately about real installed faces
      # rather than a fixture: one rasterizes `<text font-family="Arial,
      # sans-serif">` and two ask for CJK coverage. A GitHub Linux runner ships
      # neither a CJK face nor anything called `Arial` — and `fontdb` resolves a
      # family by name, so fontconfig's metric aliases do not stand in for one.
      # Installing a CJK package would answer two of the three and leave the
      # third failing for a font whose licence keeps it off this image. Windows
      # and macOS both have those faces, both run this suite, and neither is
      # weakened by a Linux runner that cannot.
      - name: test the portable crates
        run: >
          cargo test --locked
          -p bt-unicode -p bt-doc -p bt-detect -p bt-layout -p bt-persist
          -p bt-winres -p bt-transcript -p bt-viewport
          -p bt-pty -p alacritty_terminal
sampled_files.README.md: Folio is an open-source Windows terminal. It typesets LaTeX where a command prints it, previews files beside the prompt, and marks the tab of an agent that is waiting for you. [中文说明](README.zh-CN.md) · [Shortcuts](docs/shortcuts.md) · [Security](SECURITY.md) · [Changes](CHANGELOG.md) > **Preview.** 0.3.0 is a preview build, signed by Weiyi Shi — see > [Download](#download) below. --- ## Download Take [`folio-0.3.0-windows-x64.zip`](https://github.com/lulu-loopp/folio-terminal/releases/download/v0.3.0-preview/folio-0.3.0-windows-x64.zip) from the [releases page](https://github.com/lulu-loopp/folio-terminal/releases), unpack it wherever you keep programs, and run `folio.exe`. There is no installer; keep the extracted files together in one folder. `SHA256SUMS.txt` is the hash of what you downloaded. Needs **Windows 10 1809 or newer, or Windows 11, 64-bit**. `folio.exe` and `folio.msix` are signed by **Weiyi Shi**, with a certificate from Microsoft's Artifact Signing service. On first run Windows may show **"Windows protected your PC"**. **"More info"** names the publisher: check that it reads **Weiyi Shi** before running it. The archive holds nine files that belong together: `folio.exe`, the two console libraries it needs to start a shell, `folio.msix` for the Explorer menu, `folio-here.cmd` for VS Code, and the licences and notices. The web preview needs the **WebView2 Runtime**. Windows 11 has it; Windows 10 usually does, and if it does not, the Evergreen Runtime is [here](https://developer.microsoft.com/microsoft-edge/webview2/). Without it everything except the web preview works, and the preview says what is missing. ## First run A machine that has never run Folio gets one card, once. It says **Welcome to Folio** and asks whether to check for updates, add Folio to the folder right-click menu, enable the PowerShell integration, and mark the tab for each of Claude Code, Codex and Copilot CLI this machine has. Update checks arrive on; the rest arrive off. Nothing about theme, font, size, language or layout — those are one click away and cost nothing while they are wrong. **Rest the pointer on a row and it says how** — including which of your own files the switch writes, and that the file is copied to a dated backup first. **Every row on the card is also a row in Settings**, so nothing on it is a last chance. **Done** applies the rows that are on. **Not now** and `Esc` keep the shipped values: the update check on, the rest off. Either way the card does not come back, and if you were already using Folio you never see it. The first tab opens the first shell your machine actually has. The five shipped profiles are looked for in order — PowerShell 7, Windows PowerShell, WSL, Git Bash, Command Prompt — and one whose program is not installed does not appear in the menus that start a shell; it stays on the Profiles page in Settings, greyed out and naming the program that was looked for. The seven agent profiles are found the same way, on the Windows path, and that is the same lookup the card's agent rows use. The PowerShell integration adds one line — `. "$env:APPDATA\Folio\shell-integration\folio.ps1"` — to the `$PROFILE` a PowerShell names for itself, after copying the file as it stood to a dated backup beside it; delete that line to undo it. Command marks and inline `$…$` formulas run on that integration. Git Bash and WSL need none of it. Where that file is comes from the shell, so a row left on when the card is answered takes effect in the next PowerShell session, and Settings > Terminal says so until it does. If you were not asked on the card, a strip offers the same thing the first time a PowerShell pane prints something: **Add to `$PROFILE`** does it, **Don't show again** ends the asking, and closing the strip decides nothing, so the next PowerShell asks once more. The three rows on the Agent page read the tool's own configuration file and report what is in it. On a new machine all three files are absent, so all three read Off. --- ## Features ### LaTeX rendering in the terminal The LaTeX a command prints is typeset where it was printed. - `$…$` and `$$…$$` in command output are set in the line the command printed them on. - The preview pane takes those, plus `\(…\)`, `\[…\]` and the bare `amsmath` environments. - Unsupported LaTeX remains visible as source text. - Inline `$…$` is told from a shell variable by the PowerShell integration below. Without it inline formulas stay as source, and `$$…$$` blocks still typeset. ### Made for agents The agent that is waiting for you is marked on its tab, so there is nothing to go and check. - A waiting agent lights a dot on its tab, flashes the taskbar if another program has the focus, and raises a Windows notification if the window is minimised or on another desktop. - One request interrupts at most once, and the dot clears when you answer in that pane or the program withdraws the request. `Ctrl+Shift+A` jumps to the longest wait. - Claude Code, Codex and GitHub Copilot CLI each have a switch on the Agent page in Settings that writes one notification hook into that tool's own configuration file and takes it back out again. Nothing is installed by default. - Seven profiles start an agent — Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Kimi Code, pi, Hermes, OpenCode — found on the Windows path; one installed inside WSL is run from the WSL profile. Any program that writes `OSC 1337;RequestAttention=yes` raises the mark, with nothing installed at all. ### Preview beside the prompt: files, PDF, video, web What is in a file is readable beside the prompt, without opening another application. - A card comes up under the pointer when it rests on a name in the files column: the PDF page by page, the video playing, the first lines of the text, the image itself. - The preview pane opens the file beside the prompt — markdown typeset, PDF page by page, video playing, a web page with an address field and Back. - A path the terminal printed opens in the preview pane on a click, and goes to the machine's own application on `Ctrl`+click. Paths nobody marked up are found too, once the file is confirmed to exist. - A web address follows the same rule: a click opens it in the preview pane, `Ctrl`+click hands it to the browser. - A window holds as many pages as it has preview panes. A second page opens on a pane of its own instead of navigating the first, so a page can be locked and another opened beside it, and a page dropped on a pane opens on the pane you dropped it on. ### Markdown you can edit where you read it A `.md` file is typed into on the page you were reading, in the typeface you were reading it in. - Click into a paragraph, heading, list or quote and it shows its own Markdown — the `#` of a heading, the `**` around a bold phrase, the `- ` in front of an item, the `> ` down the side of a quote — in the reading typeface and at the reading size, while every other block on the page stays as it reads. Leave the block and it is back to its rendered form. - A code block, a table or a formula turns to monospace source instead, because there the way the characters line up is part of what they say. - The caret moves between blocks the way it moves between lines, so there is nothing to enter and nothing to leave: arrows, `Home`, `End`, `Enter` and `Backspace` do what they do anywhere else. What you select is what you copy, and a copy out of a document you are editing brings the marks with it, so what you paste back is what was there. - `Ctrl+S` writes the file, `Ctrl+Z` takes back the last change and `Ctrl+Y` puts it again. A run of typing comes back in one press rather than a letter at a time, and the unsaved dot goes out when you undo back to your last save. - A save changes the part you edited and leaves the rest of the file identical, down to the byte. A file that names its own encoding in its first bytes — what Windows PowerShell writes is the common case — is written back in it. Line endings, trailing spaces and a missing last line break survive as they always did. - `Esc` leaves the page, and so does clicking the empty space beside the text or clicking away from the pane altogether. The page goes back to reading as a page, and the caret stays where you left it. - A file over 8 MB, and one Folio could not read as text all the way through, opens and reads and copies as before but is not edited; the foot of the pane says why. - The files column's right-click menu makes a file or a folder in place: `New file…` and `New folder…` put the name field in the tree where the new row will appear, `Enter` creates it and `Esc` cancels. A name the folder will not take turns red in the field rather than being explained somewhere else. `Delete` sends a file, or a whole folder, to the Recycle Bin and asks nothing first, because the Recycle Bin is where it goes. - Right-clicking the empty space in a files column opens the menu of the folder the column is standing in, so a folder with nothing in it can still be given its first file. - `Ctrl+Shift+P` finds a file under the folder the column is standing in, and `Enter` opens it in the preview pane, ready to be typed into. ### Panes, tabs and windows that move The layout changes while the sessions inside it keep running, and all of them can be seen at once. - `Alt+Shift+-` splits a pane across, `Alt+Shift+=` splits it down. A tab or a single pane can be dragged out into a window of its own, and the panes it did not touch keep their widths. - A pane dropped on the join between two tabs becomes a tab *between* them: a gap opens where it will land. Dropped on a tab itself it joins that tab's layout. The horizontal strip, the vertical rail and the card column all read the join the same way. - `Ctrl+Shift+Z` turns the tab strip into a column of cards, one per tab, each drawing that tab's own panes in the layout they have. - `Ctrl+Shift+G` turns the files column into a Git panel: branch, working tree, staged and unstaged files, the commit graph, and a selected file's diff in the preview. - `Ctrl+Shift+↑` and `Ctrl+Shift+↓` step between commands in the scrollback, and a command that failed is marked as having failed. - The folder button over the files column lists the folders your shells are standing in, then the last five folders you pointed a column at, each marked `recent`. ### A terminal on a hotkey One key brings a terminal down over whatever is on the screen, and the same key takes it away again. - ``Win+` `` drops a terminal across the top of whichever screen the pointer is on, over whatever was standing there. Pressing it again puts the window away and hands the keyboard back to the program it came down over. - It is the same Folio — tabs, panes, the files column, the preview, every shortcut — and it keeps its shells and its scrollback between summons. - A rectangle you move or resize by hand is remembered for the display it is on, so the summon comes down where you last put it on that screen. - It has no icon of its own, and closing the last window you can see ends the run. - **Settings > Summoned terminal** holds the key, which profile a new tab opens on, the height, width and the gap below the top of the screen, whether the window hides when the keyboard leaves it, and a command to run on the first summon of each run. - At the next launch a pinned tab's last command can come back typed at its prompt — typed, and not run. ### Search everything One box answers five questions at once, and `Enter` goes straight there. - `Ctrl+Shift+P` raises a box over the top of the window with five sections that never mix: what Folio can do, the panes and tabs this window has open, the commands it has run, the files under the folder its column is standing in, and the settings. - Typing narrows all five together and the arrow keys walk them. `Enter` on a pane raises it, on a file opens it in the preview pane, on a setting opens Settings at that row, and on an action does it. - A command still running is pointed at with a ring around the pane it is running in, rather than a scroll to a line that has gone past. - File search covers the folder the files column is showing. ### Windows integration - **Settings > General > Explorer context menu** puts Folio in the folder right-click menu, and On is everything your Windows can do. Windows 11 files "Open Folio here" under "Show more options"; on Windows 10 it stands in the only menu there is. On a Windows 11 with `folio.msix` beside `folio.exe`, On also puts "Open in Folio" on the page Windows 11 opens first. Off takes back whichever is registered, and the line under the row says which of them On reaches on your machine. A running File Explorer reads its list of first-page entries when it starts, so if "Open in Folio" is not there yet, sign out and back in. `docs/PRIVACY.md` lists what is written. If Folio is already running, the entry opens the folder as a new tab in the window you used last and brings that window forward — it asks for a terminal in a folder, not for another Folio, so it does that whatever **Settings > General > Opening Folio again** says. Starting Folio any other way opens a window, unless that row says otherwise. - Windows PowerShell 5.1 ships PSReadLine 2.0.0, which misplaces the input line after the window is resized. Folio carries a patched 2.4.6 and installs it into your module path on request. On a machine whose execution policy is still the stock `Restricted`, the switch says so and hands you the `Set-ExecutionPolicy` command that lets the module load. ### Visual Studio Code `folio-here.cmd` ships in the archive, beside `folio.exe`, and is one line: ```bat @"%~dp0folio.exe" --from-here --cwd "%CD%" ``` Point VS Code's external terminal at it — Settings, or `settings.json`: ```json "terminal.external.windowsExec": "C:\\Tools\\folio\\folio-here.cmd" ``` **Terminal > Open in External Terminal** (`Ctrl+Shift+C`) then opens Folio on the folder the editor is standing in. The `.cmd` exists because that setting runs a command with no arguments, and `--cwd` is how Folio is told where to start; `--from-here` says that this is a terminal in a folder rather than another Folio, so it arrives as a tab in the window you used last whatever **Settings > General > Opening Folio again** says. --- ## Privacy Folio has no telemetry, no analytics and no crash reporting. There is no model and no API key in it; it serves the agents you already run. Two things reach the network: a page you open in the web preview, and the update check. The update check is one `GET` of `https://api.github.com/repos/lulu-loopp/folio-terminal/releases`, at most once a day across every window, carrying a `User-Agent` of `Folio` and nothing else: no version, no identifier, no query string. What it can do with the answer is draw a mark on the settings gear and a line in Settings; it downloads nothing and replaces nothing. Switch it off at Settings > General > **Update check**, or with `"update_check": false` in `settings.json`. What it remembers lives in two directories: `%APPDATA%\Folio` for settings, profiles, schemes and the session, and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Folio\WebView2` for the web preview's cookies and cache. Delete the first and Folio starts as it did new. ```powershell Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:APPDATA\Folio" Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Folio\WebView2" ``` What is in each file, and why a full address ends up in `session.json`, is in [`docs/PRIVACY.md`](docs/PRIVACY.md). ## Known issues - **A window was once reported drawing its top half black** after a move to a second monitor, unreproduced. Attach `%APPDATA%\Folio\diagnostics.log` if you hit it. - **`.webm` needs the VP9 or AV1 Video Extension** from the Microsoft Store. A stock Windows has neither, and without one there is no still and no playback. - The rest are in [`CHANGELOG.md`](CHANGELOG.md). ## Licence MIT or Apache-2.0, at your option. Every dependency's licence and the notices they require are in [`THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md`](THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md). The two licences grant copyright and patent permissions and nothing else. The Folio name and the marks are not covered — [`TRADEMARK.md`](TRADEMARK.md) says what that means for a modified distribution. ## Building and contributing Building from source is in [`docs/BUILDING.md`](docs/BUILDING.md); [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md) is how a change gets made; security reports go through the private channel in [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md), not an issue. ## What's next - macOS, then Linux. - The terminal from a phone. These are directions, not dates.

repository.readme:
# Paperraft

AI research briefs for deciding what to read, test, and build.

Paperraft is the public name of the project. The `ai-radar` repository, command
names, storage keys, and existing URLs remain compatible.

Briefs with pending analysis include an editorial reading guide selected by
research area. These authored prompts help readers inspect the paper and plan
a comparison; they do not populate the evidence model or imply that a test was
run. Existing deep reports supply findings and test steps when available.

[![tests](https://github.com/lusknchars/ai-radar/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/lusknchars/ai-radar/actions/workflows/tests.yml)
![python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.12+-3572A5)
![deps](https://img.shields.io/badge/runtime_deps-5-8957e5)
![frontend](https://img.shields.io/badge/frontend-no_framework,_no_build-1f6feb)
![llm](https://img.shields.io/badge/judge-Kimi_K3_or_Claude-d4a373)
![status](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-pre--1.0-db6d28)

Paperraft collects arXiv papers on efficient inference and agent harnesses, counts how many **independent** GitHub repositories implement each one, and publishes a daily digest plus a self-contained web archive. The archive opens with 30 concise paper briefs; a paper worth more attention can be expanded into a full-text report on demand. Papers that already broke out in attention are cut on purpose — the point is to find what nobody has looked at yet.

The newsletter foundation adds separate recent-paper and implementation-signal
selections, explicit collection freshness, reliable Telegram retries, and a
weekly English email draft built from existing briefs. A private signup service
supports confirmed email subscriptions through Resend. Setup, current limits,
and the work required to activate live delivery are documented in
[`docs/newsletter-foundation.md`](docs/newsletter-foundation.md).

![Paperraft](assets/banner.svg)

## Deploy to Vercel
